utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. I apologise for the delay, and before we hear the next witness, I believe there is something that the Defence would like to bring to the attention of this Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, there is. There is just two matters. The first one doesn't concern this witness and the second one does. The first one is just an inquiry that we need to have resolved and that is relating to the provision of the expert report. The Prosecution in the past had an expert report which formed part of the materials, and there's been some discussions with the Prosecution at an earlier stage about what would happen with respect to that expert. Now we're coming to the break, or a break, anyway, not the break but a break, just prior to the end of the Prosecution case, and if there is going to be expert evidence led by the Prosecution now, then it's getting to the stage where we need the report because in the break we'll -- we'll consider it. It's to be hoped that we wouldn't need any extra time and if we got the -- if we got the thing now or within the next couple of days we'd be in a position to proceed and we'd be -- we wouldn't ask for any more time, but obviously with expert evidence you need to get your own expert opinion and need to have the proper chance to take instructions and, generally speaking, to deal with it. So might I just ask the Prosecutors now to indicate what is happening with this -- with the expert and -- and what's the future of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's deal with those two things one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Your Honour, as we discussed at the meeting we had, the meeting in room 177 concerning the expert report, we were waiting for Mr. Karavelic to testify and then we would see the expert after Mr. Karavelic testified. The meeting that we had three weeks ago, and that was the discussion then and that's the same statement now. We're waiting for Mr. Karavelic to complete his testimony, then we have to go see the expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. So it implies that in this week you will be in the position to inform the other party whether there will be a new expert report or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We should be able to by the end of the week. But once again we've got to have Mr. Karavelic testify. That was the final military witness that we needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we'll see what occurs about that. Obviously the more timely the better. Your Honours, the next matter concerns the witness to come. That's Ms. Kate Adie. Now, we've received proofing notes in respect of that witness. I'm not sure if Your Honours have those proofing notes. I wouldn't be referring to them in detail now but I just want to raise my concerns about a couple of matters here. The first is that there appears to be, at least by reference to the proofing notes, some sort of intention to call opinion evidence from this witness about whether there was a massacre or not. Now, I'm not sure exactly how my friend is proceeding -- wishes to proceed about that, but I wish to say that I would object to any general evidence being given by this witness on that topic at all. I don't object to the witness saying what she saw, what she noticed, but -- and what she noticed about particular persons who were dead. She might say, "Well, I saw a particular wound on them. I've seen that sort of wound before. I'm not a pathologist but I've seen gunshot wounds and this looked like a gunshot wound." I don't wish to be unrealistic about it. Of course she can say what she saw. But to give opinion evidence, to give opinions there really has to be a proper basis laid and as far as I can see here what's -- the basis that seems to be being laid is that she's an experienced journalist who has received some wounds herself and has watched conflicts and there are various other experiences that she's had over the years which I referred to in the proofing notes, and what I want to raise is this, Your Honours, that if there is sought to be crime scene opinion evidence given, wherein it's not good enough to give it to us in proofing notes the day before. If she is to become a witness who is going to give expert opinions about bullet marks in walls or shell craters or their absence or the cause of particular fires, then we need to know that in advance. And with respect, at the moment what was going to be a very short cross-examination, quite frankly, is -- is now likely to take significantly longer, but in any event, I'm going to be objecting to general opinions being given. Now, Your Honours can't rule on this now and I just want to place it on the record that that's what's going to happen. I'm going to be objecting to that so everyone knows in advance what's coming. And it is a matter of importance that people qualify themselves as experts as able to say something that you the Tribunal are not in a position to work out for yourselves just by using human intelligence and experience. Now if there is such a field of expertise it has yet to be established. I don't know what it is and I don't know what the qualifications are, but on what we've been provided with there is no way in the world this witness qualifies as an expert of any sort. So therefore I'll be objecting. If there's anything more by way of expertise to come we better hear about it before the witness comes, Your Honour. So that's what I'm raising now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any reply from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have no intention of asking her for her opinion as to whether or not a massacre occurred. I've never heard of such in evidence this Tribunal and I don't expect to lead such evidence. With regard to her observations, we will be asking her as to her observations. Some will -- based on her experience will border on some sort of expertise but overall her basic observations, what she saw. At times did she see any crater holes? What the inside of an apartment with dead people looked like? Those are basic observations that people make. In addition to that, as Your Honour knows, in other cases experienced war journalists or war correspondents have been given the opportunity to make all sorts of opinions. As this Court knows, Paul Davies from ITN news who testified in the Strugar trial and the Milosevic trial offered opinion evidence as to the types of weaponry that was used by the JNA and the Croatian armies. The various -- the differences in strengths between two armies, the abilities of the armies to attack targets and strike them, the types of -- the types of shells that were used to damage or rockets that were used to damage certain items, the weaknesses of the various armies. In the Galic case, Morten Hvaal, which is H-v-a-a-l, the photo journalist from Norway testified about persons shot, the pattern of shooting, the types of death that were caused as a result of blood loss due to people being shot, in blood loss, Van Linden of Sky Television in the Galic case testified as to areas of sniping, the direction of shots being fired, whether or not civilians were being targeted. So what has happened in this Tribunal is that experienced war correspondents who have covered war after war or conflict after conflict who have seen people die in front of them, who have seen all sorts of attacks and battles occur right in front of them, have been given some sort of leeway to discuss certain types of facts and offer some opinion evidence. But with regard to cause of death, with regard to whether or not a massacre occurred, I'm not asking her to testify to those types of issues. Whether or not she saw wounds and described the wounds, yes. She'll say that "I saw what I thought were bullet wounds." Whether when she walked into a room and what did you see inside the room? "Well, other than behind the victims where there were a few bullet holes, the rest of the room was intact. The windows were intact. The houses were intact. There was no rummaging or trashing of the house." Those types of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that in some jurisdictions the opinion, views from a fact witness, is not allowed. However, this is an International Tribunal. It is not a jury trial. The Judges will decide on a case-by-case basis whether it goes to the special area of expertise and whether the witness is capable to testify in that area. So generally speaking, all the questions and the answers should be within what the witness saw or she noticed during that time. However, we'll also give some leeway to certain areas. It all depends on the actual situations during the proceedings. Anyway, we'll try to see if it's workable or not. So could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please stand up and make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. The witness is yours. Examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you state your name, please?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: My name is Kate Adie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what country do you live?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: In the United Kingdom, in Britain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you do for work?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I'm a journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many years have you ban journalist?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: About 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who do you work for at this time?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I've worked freelance for the BBC. I've worked for the BBC for those 30 -- 33 years, and my final job was as the chief news correspondence for BBC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the chief news correspondent what sort of matters did you cover?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I covered all major stories, not exclusively warfare. Terrorism, major trials, and major incidents, those at home and abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to warfare, what wars had you covered?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I covered the conflict in Iran/Iraq, the civil war in Lebanon, numerous wars and conflicts in Africa, Sierra Leone, Chad, Angola, conflict -- the war when the Russians were in Afghanistan, Chechnya, and several smaller conflicts, Central America, the Falklands war, I went with the army and in fact joined the British army for the Gulf War in 1990 and spent six months in the army and was present with the invasion troops going into Iraq and then Kuwait, and then I was in southern Iraq at the end of the invasion two years ago. And then I spent four and a half years often on -- in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll gets to the former Yugoslavia shortly. Did you cover any terrorist incidents?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Scores of terrorists incidents. Apart from having covered the conflict in Northern Ireland for some 25 years from the early 70s, which involved an enormous array of terrorists incidents, bombings, shootings, ethnic -- well, as it were, a kind of ethnic cleansing. Also the Red Brigade in Italy, ETA in the Basque country in Spain, the PLFP, the Palestinian -- the many Palestinian liberation and terrorist groups operating in the 1970s and 80s, and the Black September, the PLO, across the Middle East and Europe for some 15 years from the early 1970's until the late 1980s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time that you covered these various conflicts were you ever injured?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Several times, but mainly in former Yugoslavia with quite serious injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us how you were injured?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I've been hit by bullets four times. Extraordinarily lucky, just grazed taking bullet fragments and taking shrapnel fragments as well. One of those incidents was in China, one was in the Middle East, and then three of them in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated you were in Bosnia and the war in the former Yugoslavia. When did you serve in the -- or report on the war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, when did I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Report on the war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I first went to Slovenia at the very start of the break-up of former Yugoslavia. In fact, I remember reporting on seeing the first tank operational in Europe, well, technically since the Second World War but you could say that, I suppose, the Hungarian uprising and Berlin saw tank operations, but I saw almost the first tank coming through a cabbage field in Slovenia at the very start of the conflict when Slovenia broke away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Croatia? Did you cover the Yugoslavian Croatian war?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I immediately moved on to the Croat-Slav -- -Serb war and I saw action in most of the major areas, in the Krajina, and around the border areas and the river and in the area of Vukovar, Osijek, Pakrac, all the major centres. Intense skirmishing, I think we would call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I moved on to the war in Bosnia and was based in several places over a period of some three years. In Sarajevo and in the Lasva Valley, in the Kiseljak and Vitez-Zenica area, working though to other places such as Mostar and Tuzla and Bihac. All the major -- and Gorazde. All the major areas of conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say you covered the war from 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you receive any special training while you served in the British army during the Gulf War?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I was -- all of us who were actually in the army as journalists were trained to act as battlefield medics and were given intensive training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever serve as a medic in any of these conflicts or wars?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I don't know if I served, but I certainly saw a lot of people who were injured, badly, and in some cases had the opportunity to intervene, colleagues who were injured and also civilians with various injuries and wounds and gave them first aid, intensive first aid and sometimes got them to some sort of hospital, and -- and this is not the first time. I've done it in other wars as well. And also, specifically in Sarajevo during very intensive shelling I have been present twice at the hospital, the main hospital in Sarajevo, and directed triage in the emergency area. Such was the chaos with over -- in one instance, a hundred badly injured people coming to the hospital in under an hour and having to be examined and either taken to surgery or made to wait.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in that case you indicated that you directed the triage. What exactly did you do?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: It means you have chaotic scenes with hysterical, injured, and people in extreme states of pain and distress coming in with their friends and relatives in -- while shelling is still going on in the hospital within that area. And in the chaos, you have to decide what the limited facilities for surgery can deal with and direct the most seriously injured cases and make the other cases wait or possibly get them some minor attention from anybody who is around. But these are chaotic circumstances, but you need to examine people very quickly and work out what their injuries are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen persons with shrapnel injuries?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I have lost count of the occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about persons with gunshot injuries?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Again, hundreds of times. I was also -- I have been to hospitals in Afghanistan, Iraq, and also in Beijing in China during the Tiananmen Square after the demonstrations were broken up by the army, where I saw several hundred people with gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on. Let's move to Bosnia in September 1993. Could you tell us where you were?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I was based in the Lasva Valley near the town of Vitez operating down to Sarajevo, Mostar, Jablanica, Zenica, in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the morning of September 15th, do you recall where you were?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: In Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who else was present?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I had a small team, a cameraman, a producer, and a satellite, couple of satellite engineers. There were one or two other press around. It was used, Vitez, as a press base, mainly because of the presence of the British army which had a main base in Vitez, and we liaised with them regularly. We worked sometimes alongside them. We didn't work for them, but we worked alongside them and they were very open with their information to us, some of which was operational information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you learn anything that morning?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: They had had reports, the British army had had reports of an incident near or involving the town of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else did they tell you about that incident?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: They suggested that a number of people had been killed and that it was not what one might call a running incident. In other words, where there had been an exchange of fire between militias. These were civilians who had been killed, and they knew that they -- that there was -- there were some bodies which could be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you where the bodies were that could be seen?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: They had been informed and had a message. I don't know where it came from, but clearly from someone in Prozor, that some bodies were actually in Prozor, the town there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We decided to go. Not an automatic decision, because you had to judge each piece of information on its merits and sometimes information could be misleading, sometimes turned out not to have any -- any kind of substance behind it. There used to be a lot of stories circulate in Bosnia. We were well aware after three years in the country that some stories had no basis in truth. This one, though, did sound as if it had substance, and Prozor was not too difficult for accession. That's another decision. We have perhaps ahead of us a whole day available to get the story, so we have to calculate whether we could actually get there, get pictures, television insists on getting the pictures, and also we had to assess the risk, which in Bosnia was always a very difficult task because the press used to be possible targets for all factions in Bosnia. The roads had many roadblocks on them at the time manned by various militias, sometimes civilians, often drunk, and there were also mines, sniper fire, artillery positions, and bandits who operated, thieves and bandits, considerably. Just to the north of Prozor just between Prozor and Vitez there was a notorious area which had a number of armed gangs who set upon anyone who ventured that way. So you take a very careful decision to go somewhere and this story sounded as if it had substance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you go there?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We went down to Prozor via Gornji Vakuf. We possibly met up -- I can't remember, forgive me, I can't remember precisely whether the army, the small army group which set out for Prozor went from Gornji Vakuf to the south of us or whether it went from Vitez. The road from Vitez was not too difficult to Gornji and we checked that there was no trouble on the road that morning. We drove down there. I drive an armoured vehicle. I had with me a cameraman. Just two of us. That's a team, two people which we take into dangerous situations so that one could get the other out of trouble. We don't take any more than two, and we picked up, I think, an army group, a small unit of British army soldiers with a Gurka captain, Captain Bullock, and we headed down to Prozor, which is a good road, a good run, and was kept clear much of the time because it was one of the main supply routes north to south in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once you arrived in Prozor, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We were directed to a kind of hall. I suppose you'd call it a village hall. I don't know what its function was. It was a large room. The door was open. There was quite a bit activity outside. The town the Prozor wasn't particularly lively. It had had, oh, almost half its buildings burned early on in the war, the side of the town which had been Bosnian Muslim, and there were few if any Bosnian Muslims in the town. It was almost entirely Croat. We went to this hall. There were a number of people around, some men in uniform, Croats, a number of women in traditional dress, a number of perhaps officials. I think there was a doctor there. We went into the hall and there were, and I counted them, 22 bodies on the floor. They were covered with blankets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remove the blankets and get a chance to look at them?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I didn't do that immediately. I took some general shots of the hall, what we call GV, GV, general visions, general shots of the hall. I then indicated that I wanted to look closer because it's a sensitive business and you are careful when there are corpses involved. You must always be aware of the people who are standing around. There were clearly some grieving and very distressed people. But in Bosnia generally there usually was no great objections to you going and taking a closer look at a corpse. There wasn't too much sensitivity on any side, with any religion. I indicated that I was going to do that, and I pulled, gently pulled the blankets back to look and see. The reason I do this is not because we desire pictures close up. In fact, in the BBC we don't take those for transmission. But you are looking to see what has happened to these people, because this is from a firm belief in eyewitness broadcasting, that you yourself must verify what you can. You cannot always rely on other people, particularly in a war situation where people may not tell the truth for a very good reason. So you do yourself. And although it seems distasteful for a reporter to do this, I thought it proper to inspect as well as I could the bodies. I pulled back the blankets. From what I could see, there were bullet wounds to these people, all of whom were elderly. There was one child. I couldn't estimate the age of the child, but there were -- the rest, 21 of the corpses were of elderly people. What do I mean by elderly? I don't know, 60s, 70s. They were village people by their clothes, wearing -- women with some headscarves, with home-knitted cardigans, sweaters, shawls. The men with fairly rough suits, open-neck shirts. They were village people, elderly, and I didn't inspect -- look at all the corpses. Maybe half a dozen. They all had bullet wounds. Some had one, some had two. They had been shot in the torso. I cannot remember a bullet wound to the head. I would have noticed that. But most were shot in the torso.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said they were village people based on their closing. Could you tell us about the footwear that they had?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: A lot of them did not have shoes on. That doesn't surprise me, because in both Bosnian, Croat Muslim and Serb homes, not just Bosnian Muslim homes as the idea might be, that they take their shoes off to go into the house. In nearly all country areas people wore heavy shoes or boots, and it was good manners and also good housekeeping in a muddy village to take your shoes off and leave them on the doorstep. That would be normal. And then some people would put on light slippers, leather slippers, just what we could call mules. You just push your feet in them, easily slipped off. Or in many cases elderly people would have thick knitted stockings and they wouldn't use shoes at all. So it occurred to me that these people had been indoors. So it wasn't unusual they weren't missing their shoes; they had been indoors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have any discussion with anyone there as to when these deaths occurred?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I did not have an interpreter, I should point out. Sometimes I travel with an interpreter, but as we were clearly crossing -- well, crossing boundaries, no real obvious front lines in this area, and there was big trouble with both Croat and Muslim communities all over the area at the time. The Lasva Valley was in open warfare between some Muslim and Croats communities. I did not have an interpreter because I could not find anyone who was willing to go from one area to another. Though they were brave people, the interpreters, they did and we had to say as well, take the decision that they couldn't go if we didn't know where we were going to end up, if we doesn't guarantee which group we were going to see. So I didn't have an interpreter. I understand a certain amount of Serbo-Croat, a very rough amount which I picked up, and I used to listen to conversations, but not enough for accurate translation and certainly not enough to ask questions and conduct a conversation. But the army had an interpreter, and through that interpreter from, I think a couple of local people and one or two of the men in uniform who were standing around, we picked up that these people came from a nearby village. We got the name of the village, and that it was indicated that something had happened yesterday, because when I go in anywhere, I'm looking, you know, in a very basic way, for facts. I want to know who is involved. I want to know where it happened, when it happened where it happened. Very simple questions. On the subject of when, people said yesterday. It's always a difficult one in Bosnia. Yesterday to some communities, particularly village people, sometimes means last week, even ten years ago. You have to be very careful on making assumptions about words. But I looked at the bodies, again, and they looked to me, I would say, as if it was only a 24-hour period in which they'd been killed. The blood had not gone to the base of the bodies. I know they'd been moved so that would have changed their configuration, but they looked as if the blood had not sunk. Perhaps 24, maybe at the most 36 hours by the look of them. So yesterday something had happened. And the Croats alleged that the Muslims had come into the village and that they had done this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at that hall in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Probably 20 minutes, half an hour at the most. There was no point in hanging around, and anyway, I think both myself and I think also the army captain took the view that we ought to go to the village as soon as possible to see if there was anything else happening there or what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you drive to the village of Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We drove to Uzdol. I drove an armoured vehicle along with a small number of army vehicles. It was a journey without incident, and there was discussion as to how to get there. Prozor is only about ten miles, 15 kilometres from Uzdol, but it's a long and winding set of lanes. I mean, typical high set of cluster of hamlets. We went through one or two hamlets on the way. There was an argument as to precisely what route we were taking. It wasn't a direct road, but we had no incidents on the way there, and it was a climb to a village quite high in the hills to the east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see anything along the way just outside of Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Just outside Uzdol as we were nearing it, and we knew because we had very detailed maps, we used army ordnance survey maps so I knew where I was going. I wasn't in contact with the army. We don't have radio contact, but I was reading a map and my cameraman was driving and then we swapped over. I was driving because as I near any operational area, I always drove and the cameraman was there waiting to film. And he was also looking at the map and we knew we were very near and we could see towards the top of the ridge a big white building which we knew was probably the central -- the school. We'd been told that that was a rendezvous point by the army. And we must have been a mile -- now I can't be accurate, but within sight of the village we both spotted out in a green field, it was late summer, that there was something in the field approximately 50, 60 yards from us. We stopped the vehicle. The cameraman got out, used his lens to close-up on this, and he said "It's a body." I looked through it. It was a body. We didn't approach it because there might have been a booby-trap. You can't be too careful. We didn't know what we were going into. We had no idea. You keep an open mind so you are extra careful. And then there was a second body, we thought, in another field a bit further up. We took pictures of both. Then we got back in the vehicle and went on to the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when did you arrive within the village of Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: About 11.00-ish in the morning. I can't be accurate. I wasn't looking at the time. It was coming towards the hottest part of the day, I do remember. It was a hot September day, and it was very bright sunshine that day. It was nearing midday, 11.00, midday-ish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do once you got to the village?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I have a system in which, unless it's necessary for security reasons, by that I mean we are under threat, physically being shot at or there is a very present threat, I don't automatically accompany soldiers. I don't think that's right. I'm a journalist. I'm independent of them. So while they went to certain houses, having said to us, you know, watch out for booby-traps, but they were rare, rare. They did happen sometimes but we had a feeling that this wasn't an instance where we would find that. We headed for the first few houses we saw. Most of the doors were open, and so we decided we'd go and look inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any procedure or any plan or policy that you use when you go out and look at houses or look in areas where there have been killings?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I'm looking for facts. I'm looking for the straightforward pictures which tell me what has happened. I'm looking for the circumstances. I'm looking at all the detail. I'm not just looking for bodies. I've spent quite a lot of time in various countries well before this learning that things are sometimes not what they seem, that bodies can be placed around. I remember that in the Iran/Iraq war. One of the protagonists used to take a truck and regularly throw corpses off the back of it in certain areas to look as if there had been a fight and dump corpses. You can go to other places where you discover that bodies have been dragged from one place to another. So you are automatically suspicious, wary, careful. I'm looking to see if there has been a fight. I'm looking to see what might have happened. I'm trying to get, of course, because the next thing I'll be looking for is eyewitness accounts from people alive who were around at the time. But as this village appeared to have nobody in the streets at all, that we were -- was very obvious, there were no animals out, there were no dogs barking, there were no chickens, nothing to be seen, no cows in the field. The place had a look of being empty, and there were no people. There were no children running to see us. That would have been automatic. There was nothing. There was nothing. So we went -- before we even got into the houses I remember in a group it's a higgledy-piggledy hamlet with houses here and there, not a straight line. We already saw that outside one house there was a corpse on the steps of a house, and we filmed that. Then we went into the first house. We were next -- and I can't remember the sequence, I'm afraid now. I can't remember the sequence, but we went into house after house, and the scene in each house was that we discovered dead people, sometimes one, sometimes two. Sometimes in the front room, these are small houses, on a sofa, on the floor. I went into one house and there was a body in bed, and the bedclothes were soaked through with blood. I went into another house. There was a body in the corner. There was a huge blood spray up the wall, a white wall. And all of these people were elderly, all of them. There were a couple in a barn. The army found them and called me over, and there was a man and a woman. He was lying on top of her, embracing her, as if to protect her. Both had bullet wounds. Every single corporation I looked at had bullet wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many houses did you inspect?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Sixteen, 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe the interior of these homes?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Neat little country homes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. I'm sorry. Your Honours, I object to that. The witness can describe individual homes one by one. There is no such thing as a general home, and the witness ought to be asked to explain one by one the houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could deal with the general matters. Then we could have specific house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's true but there are specific dead persons named on the indictment that we have to deal with, and it's those people that -- that I'm proposing to deal with anyway, Your Honour. But if Your Honours think it's useful, that's Your Honour's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's begin with the general impression and then we'll go to the specific houses if possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The houses that you went into, could you tell us generally what they looked like?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I've been into hundreds of Bosnian, Croat, Muslim and Serb houses. I mean, it would only be fair it seems to me to describe what is common to them that might be useful in that they tend to be -- they tend to be neat and tidy, and very -- there is nearly in every house a little china or ornament cabinet. That's very common to each family. Full of their trinkets, their best coffee set. That would be common to the whole of Bosnia, the whole business of offering coffee to visitors is a tremendous tradition. There would be the best coffee set. There would be also sometimes -- in a Croat house there would be religious icons in the sense of a small picture of the Virgin Mary or a crucifix or little pictures. That would be common to Croat homes. In Muslim homes there would often be also imagery in the sense of pictures of certain places. In Serb homes often pictures of and little ornaments relating to Serb saints. It was a classic, sort of what I would call rather old-fashioned kind of display. There would also always be shoes on the front doorstep. Most people would take their outer shoes off. And inside you would find a living room very much like a Western living room with sofas, very heavily carved wooden furniture. I mention this because during attacks the splinters from wood from the furniture, from heavy furniture of wardrobes and sofas, and beds would be lethal. In Sarajevo I have been frequently in one of those rooms, and then if anything hits in the splinters from the wood go everywhere. So there are certain things which I thought were common to these house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the condition of those houses that you visited?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Perfectly normal. There was no sign of a fight or a struggle. That was the first thing I was looking for. Nothing was disarranged. Nothing was broken. There was nothing either in those houses damaged. Another feature, and why I mentioned the china and the knick-knacks and the little personal treasures was that there was an absolutely common feature in four years for sometimes during ethnic cleansing, as it came to be known, for all the personal ornaments to be thrown out of the place, smashed, trashed, ruined. It's a very common habit. Not just of course in the Balkans but in any area where you are trying to destroy the raison d'etre, the living conditions of people. Nothing was broken, nothing at all. There had been no fight, no signs ever struggle or resistance, nothing. Not even furniture overturned, rearranged, nothing. Which made it extremely disturbing. I mean, I thought then I could make some assumptions about how the deaths came about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any evidence of bullet spraying?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. There were two instances. One of the person in the bed and one of the body against the wall where both had been hit from clearly quite close range, and the entry point of the bullet was quite small, but the exit, we could tell with the one we looked at which was against the wall that the exit point had produced an enormous spray of tissue, body tissue, and blood right up the wall for a foot, a foot and a half, and that the bullet had exited into the wall. And this is -- I mean, it's -- it's classic bullet-exit damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a lot of bullet holes in these houses?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: A few. Not many. Most of these people had one. And in -- in some cases two bullets. I didn't examine the bodies in great detail looking for others. Again, they were torso wounds, though there was one with a very bad wound in the neck with the head partly off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any damaged wood or wood splitting which you would describe previously in -- which you would see in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No, nothing. I mean, for heaven's sake the windows were still in the house. Mean, if you fire bullets around in a place or you have any kind of a firefight or explosion, I mean, the windows go. That's automatic. All the glass was in the windows. All the china was on the window sill. All the china was in the little cabinets. There was no damage at all. That's why we need -- hadn't even been a struggle. Nobody had knocked anything over. There was nothing in any way to suggest anything other than close-range firing of bullets nor had there been much run-up. There was not a spray of bullets in the wall. It looked as if the rifles, I'm assuming they were AK47s, which were the commonest weapon. I don't know, I have no idea about that. But whatever had been used was not on spray. It was not on full automatic. It had been on single shot or repeat shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, outside of these homes did you see any shelling damage or any craters?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Not a single shred of evidence. No craters on the road, no damage to houses, no holes in walls, no holes in roofs, nothing. No sign whatsoever. Nothing. And also had there been artillery pieces or mortar positions, the British army which would have sent out a certain amount of surveillance, would have reported back to us of such positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you take any video of these 16 or 17 homes?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you finished taking the video of those homes, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We went up to a larger building on the -- on the ridge, a white building which we were told was a school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe the interior of that.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: It was empty. It was rather curious. There were also bloodstains on the walls inside, in the main hall. They looked as if they had been -- someone had attempted to perhaps clean the place up. I could not get any clear picture of what happened in this building. There were no bodies there. I could not find anybody who -- there was no one in the village who appeared to have been there and was still alive. There were no eyewitnesses that I could discover. We asked people around who had come with us. There did not appear to be anyone I could get an eyewitness report from, which is a major problem for a journalist. I can't substantiate. I don't like to speculate too much. I could, but all I could see was a room where there was blood on the walls an attempt to clean it, and quite a lot of bullet marks around. Again, bullets, nothing else. The roof was intact. The windows were in. Again, just gunfire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there any Croatian soldiers present?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There were some Croats in military uniform. I always hesitate to designate who is what because at the time anybody could wear any piece of uniform. There were some Croats in military fatigues. They had come with us from Prozor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you learn anything or did you receive any information as to what occurred at this school?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Both down in Prozor and up in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There were remarks. There were comments that, first of all, the Bosnian Muslims were to blame, that they had come to the village. There appeared to be a complication, and it was impossible to pin down precisely what had happened. The impression I got was that there was some form of revenge act taking place. There had been clearly some kind of action between fighting men, men of military age, in other words young men with guns, not villagers but young men with guns, that there had been some kind of action and at some point the Muslims had come into the village. And it looked to us as if the Croat fighting men were no longer there, because as I said there was no evidence where the elderly people died of any action, any crossfire. It looks as if they may have left the village, I say may have left the village. I can't substantiate that. And that the elderly people were killed by men with guns who went from house to house quite quickly, not doing any looting or damage or trashing anything. But as I say, there may have been some action beforehand of which I still cannot pin down. I can find no one to verify what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during your visit to Uzdol, did you take any video? Did the cameraman take any video?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We took extensive amounts of video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many minutes of video was taken between Prozor and Uzdol or the two together if you wanted to total that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Oh, probably -- I probably had two cassettes and they probably had ten to 12 minutes on each at the most, which would also have included rather lengthy interviews which were cut down for the transmission with one of the EU monitors. There were two EU monitors with us. One of them was a Dutchman. I can't remember the other one's nationality. He may have been Greek but I'm not sure. One -- the Dutch monitor, Rudy Gerritsen, I interviewed them. I also interviewed one of the Croat men in uniform who claimed that he knew the identity of two of the victims, was related to them. That's not unusual in the sense that nearly all the militias and people were local to their area. He very likely -- he clearly knew the village when he was showing people around, pointing things out. So there would be two longish interviews plus a third piece for me which we call a to-camera piece which is an explanation for the viewers. So all in all maybe 12, 15 minutes on each video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croat soldier who knew the identity of -- of two of the victims, was that the two elderly people who were found in a barn embracing?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: He called them Ratkic. The name he gave was Ratkic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was a broadcast ever made from all of this film and these interviews?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We returned to Vitez that afternoon and I cut a piece for the BBC 1800 news bulletin which was broadcast from London that night. We had a satellite transmission equipment in Vitez for direct connection to London, and we recut with very little difference a piece for the later 9.00 bulletin. So two transmissions went on the BBC. They would also go out on a great number of TV stations around the world with which the BBC has agreements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour with the Court's permission I'd like to show the first of the two videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's about three minutes long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We will be using Sanction because it's a video, Your Honour the Sanction system. The first video is V0002725, which is 65 ter number 140.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 373.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there's a transcript that goes with that, too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's assigned the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have the technicians place the counselled with the video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're trying to resolve the technical problem, Your Honour. They're going to send someone from the technical booth, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe we should have an early break so during the break we could have that fixed. Is that agreeable? Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And by the way, as I said that last week, we'll have an extra siting this afternoon. Well, we'll have 30 minutes break. We'll resume at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll try again. Video V000-2725.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "The village of Uzdol is high in hills of Central Bosnia. It has a school building later used as local Croat military headquarters. Yesterday, the Bosnian army descended on Uzdol, then withdrew leaving terrible evidence of their brief visit. We walked through the scattered farms and cottages with British soldiers and European Monitors trying to establish what happened here. It soon became clear that every house and cottage had been visited by the Bosnian army soldiers. Systematic slaughter. Every room had been entered. There were bullets in the bedroom walls. An old lady killed in her bed. The victims were all elderly and one child unable to flee. Some had tried to hide. One couple, 67-year-old Martin Ratkic and his wife Cara, had taken refuge in the barn. They lay in each other's arms, apparently shot by someone standing over them. "The word 'atrocity' has been used a lot in this war. It's usually very difficult to find out exactly what has happened. There is so much propaganda and myth, but in this case it seems clear that there was wholesale killing of civilians. But as to the reason, it's almost impossible for an observer to guess. "One answer came from a Croat soldier who came back to his parents' house this morning to find his mother burned in the ruins. "'It is a war. It is a war,' he said. 'They hate civilians and they hate us.' "For the UN in this instance British soldiers and the European Monitors know there is nothing they could do except to observe and report to a European committee. "Probably they will say maybe it's a war crime because there are slaughtered civilians and maybe in the future there will be an investigation of the Court of Justice in The Hague or something like that. "22 of the victims had already been taken to a makeshift morgue in the nearby town of Prozor. Again the UN and the EC observed and did not comment, very conscious of the way such incidents in this war are either distorted or denied becoming part of the propaganda of both sides with the UN being seen as a convenient scapegoat. Such was the nature of the killing at Uzdol that recriminations have not yet gathered force and grief was only beginning. "Kate Adie, BBC news, Uzdol. For ABC news this is Kate Adie of the BBC, Central Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Adie, do you recognise that film footage?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you recognise that as?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: That is the edited story, first of all, that we showed on the news, and then it was followed by some extra shots which not -- not all of which would have been transmitted for reasons of taste. Close-ups are not accepted in the BBC, close-ups of dead bodies, or lingering shots. But in this instance, we probably showed more than we normally did because of the nature of the story. And I did have conversations with the BBC in London about this, saying that unless we actually showed, as it were, the state of the bodies that we could not convey the full impact of the story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's another video. The -- there is a different intro in the beginning for the first 15 seconds. The body of it is the same, but it doesn't include that last minute at the end which has no sound. Would the Court like to see that, too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as you like. This is your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Then, fine. That is video V000-2632.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 374.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's 65 ter 942.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "Peace talks founded the Muslim forces have continued their defensive in Central Bosnia and have taken more territory by force. The massacre took place at Uzdol, 40 miles west of Sarajevo after Croat soldiers failed to hold the village and it was taken by the Muslim Bosnian army. You may find some of the pictures in this report disturbing "The village of Uzdol is high in the hills of Central Bosnia. It has a school building lately used as local Croat military headquarters. Yesterday, the Bosnian army descended on Uzdol then withdrew leaving terrible evidence of their brief visit. "We walked through the scattered farms and cottages with British soldiers and European Monitors trying to establish what happened here. It soon became clear that every house and cottage had been visited by the Bosnian army soldiers. Systematic slaughter. Every room had been entered. There were bullets in the bedroom walls, an old lady killed in her bed. The victims were all elderly and one child unable to flee. Some had tried to hide. One couple, 67-year-old Martin Ratkic and his wife Cara had been taken refuge in their barn. They lay in each other's arms apparently shot by somebody standing over them. "The word 'atrocity' has been used a lot in this war. It's usually very difficult to find out exactly what has happened, there is so much propaganda and myth. But in this case it seems that there was wholesale killing of civilians. But as to the reason it's almost impossible for an observer to guess. One answer came from a Croat soldier who came back his parents' house this morning to find his mother burned in the ruins "'It is a war. It is a war,' he said. 'They hate civilians. They hate us.' "For the UN, in this instance British soldiers and the European Monitors, there is nothing they can do except to observe and report to a European committee. "Probably they will say maybe it's because they are slaughtered civilians, and maybe in the future there will be an investigation of the Court of Justice in The Hague or something like that. "Twenty-two of the victims had already been taken to a makeshift morgue in the near town of Prozor. Again, the UN and the EC observed and did not comment, very conscious of the way such incidents in this war are either distorted or denied becoming part of the propaganda of both sides and with the UN being seen as a convenient scapegoat. Such was the nature of the killing at Uzdol that recriminations have not yet gathered force and grief was only beginning. "Kate Adie, BBC news, Uzdol."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that video clip?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you recognise that as?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: That was the 9.00 news version, the later version. It's substantially the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer both of those videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: They are admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally Ms. Adie --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, could we just get the numbers for those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first video with ERN ETV000-2725 is Prosecution Exhibit P373. And the second one with ERN ETV000-2632 is Prosecution Exhibit P374.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Adie, did anyone from the Bosnian government or military ever contact you concerning your observations in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I can never remember that happening in four years of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anyone ever make a request to you for a copy of the video?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: The same answer. There was no organisation which was competent enough or functioning enough in four years in Bosnia to even be aware of video transmissions. There was virtually no television in Bosnia. Most people had no electricity most of the time. The idea that people would be following or aware and responding was unknown on all three sides. Though I have to say people claimed to frequently. They say, "We saw this. We saw that on BBC, on CNN." You knew they had no electricity in their house, never mind television. So most of -- the claims were usually spurious. And as for a functioning system to contact journalists, that just did not exist at all. There was, from our point of view for much of the time, no functioning government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thanks very much. Cross-examined by Mr. Morrissey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you Ms. Adie. I just have some questions first of all about the nature of the information that took you to Uzdol. Did that information came directly from Croatian sources or did it come to you through military sources?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: From military sources, from the British military operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I understand this is probably triple hearsay but I'll ask you anyway. What did the British sources that contacted you tell you about where the information originally came from?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: They weren't specific. They said that it was from Prozor, which I would assume to be a Croat source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You used the term "militia" earlier on. Are you familiar with a particular organisation called the HVO?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are -- there were many different outfits operating through four years in Bosnia. They gave themselves names at times. Some of them did not have direct connections to a headquarters, some operated as local warlords, some as militias. "Militia" is a common word that we used in the BBC when we were not precisely sure which military group this was. There were many ad hoc military operations, military units functioning on all sides. HVO I would be well aware of. But before or unless I could actually verify, I would use the word "militia" generally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And at the time when you were still -- before you went to Prozor, did you make an inquiry as to whether this was the HVO you were dealing with or some other militia organisation?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Of whom would I make that inquiry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is did you make such an inquiry?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Well, who would there be to make the inquiry of? Are you asking who I called?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking whether you made any inquiry of any person there, Ms. Adie. What's the answer?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: The answer is there was no one to ask. The assumption that there were somehow official functioning sources of information is a specious one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there is no criticism of you for not asking. I just needed the fact as to whether you did ask or not.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: You don't ask when there's a vacuum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, after that time you went down to Prozor, and when you got to Prozor did you inspect the deceased people as they're depicted in the news broadcasts that have been shown?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: They're on the floor. I didn't inspect them on film for the precise reason that I don't think that our viewers expect our reporters to do that. I did it when the camera was not on and I peeled back blankets and had a look at the bodies without disturbing the bodies as much as could. There were no objections from anybody who was there, but even so, you do it quite discreetly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was there when you did that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was there when you did that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There were a number of civilians, some elderly people. It was unclear as to whether these people -- one assumed -- I assumed that they were Prozor people. No one claimed to be there from Uzdol that I remember specifically, though there were some young men also in Croat uniform there. There was a doctor, I believe, and obviously some local workers, the man with the disinfectant. Not a lot of people around, but as I say it wasn't a particularly busy town. It was semi-deserted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just in terms of the people who were present, you've indicated that there were some -- some elderly civilians, and I want to the ask you, were those elderly civilians present when you performed the inspections of the deceased bodies that you've described?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: People were wandering in and out. Nobody interfered with me and nobody took specific notice of what we did. I arrived with the British military. They commanded some respect in the area. No one expected them to do anything untoward or improper. I was with them. And it was not unknown for journalists to do this kind of thing. And as I indicated, it did not seem to in any way offend any of the factions in Bosnia. I was frequently, for example, in intensive care units and morgues, makeshift morgues around the country, and it was -- these bodies were frequently shown to us by people. The hyper-sensitivity you get in some cultures did not exist there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. And as to the presence of, I think you said young men in Croatian uniforms, did you make an inquiry as to which unit they were from?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anyone from the British forces that you were with point out which units they were from?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: They made their own report, as did the EU monitors. I have assumed that those reports are present in this court. There were official reports made by the monitors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well I'm going to give you the opportunity to consider one such later on, but I have to ask you the questions as to what you observed and the question is: Did anyone tell you whether they were a British source or a UN source that you were dealing with the HVO or some other --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: The assumption was that the HVO were operational at that area as they were in Gornji Vakuf, in Vitez, and in several other towns in the region. I had not been to Prozor in the preceding few months concerning any major incident. Prozor itself used to be relatively, relatively - and I mean that term in a very strong way - quiet, but I did not know the Prozor region intimately regarding the units operating there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. Well, then I make -- I'm ask you the question again. Did you ask which units were operating there?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Why should I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: What else would they have been on the Croat side. I'm genuinely asking you what else would they have been? There were at least three other Croat units which I knew to operate within Bosnia but it was a long distance away, some around the border with Bosnia, others in the Tomislavgrad area and to the north of Travnik. There were different groups at different times. The HVO was a generic term often used for Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of an institution called the Home Guard?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Is that the English term for something? Can you be specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is an English term for -- for an HVO unit that we've heard about in evidence here.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: And in Serbo-Croat it would be?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's domobrani?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Not a specific term that was used by journalists or by, as far as I know, the British military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I have to say in the circumstances there was such a ragtag and, shall we say, ad hoc nature with many of these units that specific names were given to everybody. They called themselves "Fighting Tigers," "the Lions of Bosnia" -- you know, there were a dozen different nicknames given to units, normally bombastic and exaggerated. So we tended to be very careful in naming units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, as to the actual deceased people that you inspected, your method of inspecting them was to peel back the -- the coverings that there were, as you've indicated. After you did that, did you notice whether these people -- these persons at Prozor were clothed or unclothed?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: They had clothes on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you remove any of that clothing?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There was no need to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just have to deal with my questions as they come, I'm sorry. Did you personally remove any clothing from those people?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There would be no reason for me to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So the answer is that you didn't; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: If you try to get clothes off a corpse it's extremely difficulty, I might add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. Do you know whether pathologists normally remove clothes from dead bodies before they perform inspections?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Because obviously they are going for an internal inspection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And to your knowledge, how do you assess whether there's post-mortem lividity on a deceased body?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There are very specific and professional levels of inspection needed if you or pathologist. I am obviously lip not a pathologist. All I would say is I have seen a great number of bullet wounds, fragment wounds, grenade, and general injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. But just dealing with the question of post-mortem lividity, did you inspect these persons to see if they had post-mortem lividity?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I saw them in the Uzdol area. I specifically looked at one body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But let's deal with Prozor right now.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No, not in Prozor. There were merely bullet wounds in Prozor, I can confirm that. Merely bullet wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in assessing this issue of post-mortem lividity with respect to the Prozor people, what you say is you didn't look for that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I looked at the pallor of their faces. I looked at how rigid they were and a number -- I was wondering -- my fascination at that point was when did this happen? And the rough guide, and nobody seemed to dispute this was that it was within the last 24, 36 hours. And that would have been my amateur guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in terms of now the numbers of people that you looked at, you indicated 22 people, one of whom was a child and the other 21 of whom were relatively, and I understand you're not attempting to use a scientific term there, but relatively --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I'm using a cultural term there. Elderly is a matter of relativity in various cultures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. Well, in any event, I don't think there's any quarrel about it. But what I wanted to be quite clear about is that those 22 were all civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say they were civilians because they were dressed in civilian clothes; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: They were also older than any group in Bosnia than, in my experience, would ever have joined any military unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told whether or not any of the older people that were -- you looked at in Prozor had weapons in their homes?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There was no one to tell us from about the village in that sense. And what you would assume and I would assume is that with knowledge of Bosnia that in many, many homes in Bosnia, country homes, a weapon was frequently kept. Elderly people, though, were unlikely to have them. It would be my experience by 1993, because what was needed by all the fighting forces was as many weapons as possible, and I met many -- saw many instances where elderly people had given their sons and their relatives weapons and there was no longer a weapon in each house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it ever pointed out to you that any of these individuals in fact owned weapons at that time in September?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There would be no one to point that out, and it would be highly unlikely that they would have other than the -- kind of the occasional shotgun. AK47s and assault rifles would not be kept by elderly people. They would much more likely have a shotgun for rural incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the people in Uzdol, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I am merely cross-referencing it with several hundred other villages that I visited in four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you ever gone Uzdol before this occasion?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prozor?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times to Prozor?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Oh, I have lost count because it was on the main supply route north to south, and I would have passed through it many times, stopped in it many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also see a number of killed soldiers or dead soldiers nearby to the place where you viewed the old people dead?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I have not made any reference to that. I don't know where that idea comes from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Not in my experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you did in fact see --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- any?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. We did not see.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot about that trouble, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologise, Ms. Adie. We have to, or I have to slow down a bit. Very well. You just made a reference in a statement to the -- to the investigators some time ago -- look, I should ask you this: Did you get a chance to look at your statement before you gave evidence here?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I had my statement validated in London on oath, and I've seen it several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, look, there's no -- this is not an attempt to trip -- trip you up, but you've made a reference here and I'm just -- I just want you to clarify -- you'd be -- you said, "I think we saw some Bosnian Croats soldiers at the morgue." Now, were you referring to living Bosnian Croat soldiers when you made that comment?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: You can see them on the video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's correct and that's what I was asking you about. Very well. So the answer is then that at that -- at Prozor you saw no dead soldiers from the Croat side or from the Bosnian army side?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No, none at all; we saw only civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you got down to Uzdol - I'm jumping ahead now - the same thing applies. You saw no dead soldiers and no dead -- no dead Bosnian soldiers and no dead Croatian soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And were you told where -- were you told that any soldiers had been killed at all?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We were aware that something had probably taken place prior to the attack on the elderly people. That which I indicated in my video, we did not know what had happened. And I therefore was not going to speculate and I left it at that. It seemed that there had been -- we knew that the school had been a Croat headquarters, so one assumed that it would be -- it would have Croat soldiers in it. This is assumption, speculation by me, and therefore, if Bosnian soldiers had come into the village, there would have been some kind of engagement, or it was quite possible that people run away, and I don't actually put that out of the question. This used to happen, though no local on either side would ever acknowledge that. So I don't know, but clearly something occurred for the Bosnians to be able to come into that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Adie, I won't ask you to speculate. We've heard some evidence about all of this already. But what I do want to ask you about is the number of killed people or dead people that you saw. You saw 22 in Prozor, apparently all civilians. How many did you see in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I think 12 or 13. I say "I think," because I didn't do a precise count at the end of the day, and they were scattered around the various buildings. And there were two in fields as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all in all as to civilians you saw on your calculation 34 or 35?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Perhaps. I can't give you the precise number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now is the area of doubt connected to the number that you saw at Prozor or the number that you saw at Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No, I counted precisely in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: A good hour, hour to an hour and a half. I would -- I think I remember. I probably wasn't longer than that. Hour and a half, maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you were there and I wasn't, so are you happy if we work on the basis of approximately an hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yeah, but my memory is fuzzy on that. I'm just calculating how much film we took and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
