utterances.text: And having a look at that you can see very clearly the right ear of that person; correct? When I say "very clear" perhaps it's a relative term.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I can't see it very clearly, but there's something there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It looks like he's got an ear anyway, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's how he looked at the time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the pathologist says that ear is off when the pathologist looks at that man, you would agreed with the inference that that ear came off after you looked at it; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I would but we are so far from it. Also the argument about the ear being off, sometimes earlobes were cut off. Sometimes an ear -- it is extremely difficult to cut off an ear, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: And there would have been a great deal of blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask for an expert opinion about that but I won't, Ms. Adie.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I would have assumed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But having a look at that -- having a look at that person in the sad date they are at any event --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Had there been a major wound around the ear I would have looked closer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you indicated earlier, I think, you would have expected to notice a considerable amount of blood.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's if it was done while they were alive, of course.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the question of the two people being in each other's arms there, are you -- it may be simply my way of looking at this but I just can't really make out an arm. Can you indicate to me an arm in that photo?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Well, his elbow is -- the right elbow is going down behind the sacking, and I think there is the slight trace of a hand possibly near the woman's black traditional costume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And -- all right. So again, this is -- this is not a criticism, it's just an attempt to ascertain what the facts are. You based the comment on them being in each other's arms on that sighting that we can see there?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: It seems unlikely to me they were placed in that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, okay. We have other evidence of what people's impressions was when they saw it and, it's okay, I won't ask you to swap speculations. But anyway you've given your evidence honestly about that. I'll move on from it, thank you. Can we go to the next part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just stop there for a moment, please. I'm sorry, could we go back to the previous sighting. Stop there. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that destroyed building that can be seen, is that one of the once we've seen at an earlier stage or not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I think that is another building. I'm unclear. I think it was another building, because we were walking down the side of another building which was substantially in better order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now can we -- yes, please, go on although we're going to stop again quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Stop there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could just go back to that little half damaged -- okay. That little damaged building, is that associated with the other bigger damaged building that we just saw or is it separate?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: You mean by ownership or by geographical --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Geographically, I mean.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I assume it is. I tend not to jumble shots when I'm editing. I just have to assume it is sequential.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right, let's press on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just stop there for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is that shot taking place? Is that Uzdol or Prozor?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is that at the school?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's play it a little further and see if you can see if it helps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hard to tell. I cannot tell, I'm afraid. The school was -- it occurred to me it looks a bigger building. I don't know. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just stop there for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about that, in terms of what building that was at. There was in a part of Uzdol named Cer two churches, an old church and a new church. Did you see those?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Absolutely no. I didn't see any of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just ask you: As to the two Ratkics that you saw that we looked at earlier - that was the couple where the calico bag was - are they included in the list of people who you looked at to see what sort of wounds they had?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I bent over the man and I noticed also there was some blood behind the woman's head. Impossible for me to say whether they -- one assumed they may have fallen into that position perhaps. I can't tell. They were obviously together or he fell perhaps onto her, I don't know. And I think there was also the mark of a bullet indentation into the wall behind the woman's head. I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, can we just play on a little bit further, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just stop there. Can we just go back a moment, please. There was a young -- a man in civilian sort of clothing gesturing there. Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the man with the black top, glasses --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Not a clue. But he clearly speaks English because the English soldiers do not speak Serbo-Croat. He may have been doing some interpreting. I cannot tell you. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have any memory of that man at all?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I may not even have physically been stood there next to the camera at that point. The cameraman is shooting things and I am doing other things in another part of the room at times, and in the short time we were there, 20 minutes or so, I couldn't give you a minute-by-minute description of my physical place, and some of the shots would be taken by my cameraman around the room. He's an experienced man. He does not get directed by me to take shots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I understand. Well, okay. What this -- we can press on, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. I think we can stop there now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going -- I will have some more questions about this in a minute. All right. Could you just indicate of those -- we've seen perhaps half a dozen killed people up to now, two of whom were the Ratkics, and one of whom was the lady on the carpet there, and then we've seen two in the field, and one under a -- under a cloth in the open somewhere. It's not quite clear where. Now, of the remaining ones, although they're not on the picture, can you tell us where they were?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: One was upstairs in a bedroom in a bed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One was lying in a bed upstairs --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- when you saw her?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what wounds did the one who was upstairs in a bed --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: It was a woman, and there was so much blood I didn't look too close. And the blood was around the shoulders and neck area. I think. Yes. I do know --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I took a quick -- there are some things -- you may think I am a hard-bitten reporter but there are some things which I just find -- this was an immensely distressing time, and I was trying to do a factual observation. There were one or two things I turned away from because I did not want to look closer myself. I didn't have the stomach for it, I have to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. But I just want to ask you about this upstairs person. Do you recall was it an internal staircase you we went up?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you went up an internal staircase, and you found a person in a bed and you looked very briefly at them but it was distressing --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes. Beds are more -- what can we call it, couch-like beds. Often in country houses they weren't four legs, but they were against walls. That's quite common, to have both benches which serve as sofas, couches, sitting and sometimes bed positions. There's quite a bit of that in the traditional houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a name provided --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- for that person?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any information provided about that person?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving from that person on, can you say where the others --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There's one on a doorstep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Was that a man or female on the doorstep?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Male. Male.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many injuries did that male have to your --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- observation?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they injured by bullets or -- by a bullet or bullets or by some other mechanism?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There was no evidence of any other mechanism being used because I was also looking for possibly close quarter, as it were, attack. The use of a knife or the use of anything else, bayonet. No evidence of that at all. No injuries to faces, no injuries to hands, which gives you the idea of combat, of people, you know, getting involved in fighting. None of that. And no scrapes or abrasions or small splinters which would indicate any large explosion. Only bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular individual on the doorstep, no name for him?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And no particular bullet wound that you can now recall?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No. Torso wound, nothing -- I'm racking my memory to think of any specific body which stood out in any way different, and it was just a consistent pattern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's keep going though. That's two. Now, of the ones that aren't displayed on the screen, what other ones can you now remember?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There must have been at least two or three others in the doorways, and there was one along in a house I didn't look at which the soldiers had looked at and said, "It's just more of the same." I remember them saying that, "more of the same." We had soldiers searching in these buildings as well and had they come across anything different or noteworthy they would have told both the officer or myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So is the position -- and I'm not being critical about this at all but I just need to be clear. Is the position this: That there were a couple of bodies or a small number of bodies which you didn't yourself see in the village but were told about by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I think I probably saw just about -- I put my head into doorways and saw what was clearly a body in -- and just looked and thought I do not need to look at each body. There is no forensic demand that I do. I had by then seen a number of bodies and consistently seen that they had been attacked in the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And as to the ones that you looked round the doorway briefly, they're not -- you don't include them in the category of those that you inspected or looked at?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Looked at briefly in the sense of knowing that there are bodies there. Again, to get a sense of the total that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. In no house did you notice any firearms, is that correct, or weapons?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Absolutely. The British soldiers would have immediately shown these and would have taken them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again I think I've asked you this already but just to make sure that I have, in no place did you see a deceased Croatian soldier or indeed a deceased Bosnian soldier?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Absolutely not. No one in military uniform was found or seen by any of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that -- now, in -- on this -- on the video. Can we just go back to the video briefly. On the video there's a depiction of a dog.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wonder if we can go along at the normal pace or we can scroll to the dog. Ms. Adie, I'm sorry, because I was working from a hard copy of the video I don't have these numbered. I wonder if we could just go forward to the -- to where the dog is depicted. It's at 3.54, I believe. If we just go forward to 3.54. Stop. Go back. I've missed something. Thank you. If we just go back to that body in the field. Thank you. That's the second of the bodies in the field. Do you notice that there is by -- does there appear to be a shoe on the ground near that body?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There appears to be a boot, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the -- that's second body that you mentioned that you --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- noticed but didn't approach?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What are you able to say about the clothing of that body?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: It isn't army fatigues. I got Nigel to look very closely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you asked him that question, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. And are you able to comment on the age of that person?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No. You cannot see anything about it at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not apparent on the photograph but just to be cautious I want to ask you: Was there any -- were you able to see from where you were or using the camera any sign of any particular wounds?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No, not from that angle except you looked towards the top and that could be congealed blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But at the time -- this is really the view you had at the time, too, isn't it, because it was the -- because you were using the camera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Uh-huh, yep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. All right. Well, let's keep moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that dog injured when you first saw it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Not that one. That was a dead dog. There were, I think, two. I'm not sure if there was a third. These two dogs dead and then a third was found by a British soldier, and it was in such a poor way that it was put out of its misery by an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to interrupt the video to go over to the E-court for a moment, please, and ask the witness be shown a document. This is DD001337, and its 65 ter number is Defence 252. Yes, sorry. Could I ask for a MFI number for this one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI 375.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The B/C/S version is on the screen at the moment. I just wonder if we could have the English version, please. Sorry. Pardon me. Wait. Don't you do anything. It may be us that are on the wrong channel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Adie, can I just ask do you have an English document or B/C/S document?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I have it in Serbo-Croat. Should I have pressed ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. It'll be -- because we -- we're used to dealing with witnesses who have to have it that way, so -- would you just tell us when you have it in English? Okay. This is a document procured by the Defence, and I just want you to comment upon it -- sorry, by the Prosecution. I'm sorry. Sorry, just excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Procured by the Defence. I'd just like you to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I haven't got it in English yet. Yes, coming clearer. I have it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document headed "Analytical Report 2, Proposal for Propaganda Action, dated 1st of September 1993," and it proposes this: "1. Show wounded domestic pets on video. A slaughtered Croatian dog will cause greater concern among English viewers than five slaughters Croats. In that respect, also show footage of a three-legged animal with a broken leg which children are taking care of," et cetera. Now, let me just ask you this: First of all, did you ever see a Croat document of this nature -- when I say "Croat," I don't mean to use Croat, an HVO document of that nature proposing propaganda methods?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No. The only time I came across -- understood propaganda methods were in the compilation of videos used on TV by all three sides who developed quite sophisticated sentimental and violent advertising means to promote their cause.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To promote the war effort, okay. Well, look, okay, I'm going to come to that in a minute. That's an area where you might be able to assist the Tribunal. As to this one, though, did it seem to be a feature of Croat -- or scenes of tragedy that you were shown by the HVO or Croats that they would feature such things?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slaughtered animals or --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Piece of fantasy from one somebody sitting at a desk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: A sophistication never seen in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to the dogs, though, where were they positioned when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: One was in -- you know, between the houses. Certainly the dog that was injured was in fact discovered within a building and was in a dark building, and I did not go in to see it because it was in a terrible state, but I heard the shot as it was killed, and it was not on show.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that you put it on show in any form, but can you recall how it was discovered or not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: A soldier was searching. All the buildings were searched by the British troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Well -- but in short, this document here, are you familiar with it or anything like it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: It sounds laughable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's -- I don't mean to be nasty about it. That wasn't really my question. Are you familiar with it--

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Well, the point is it does not link -- it does not relate to the reality that I witnessed on the ground. That's my point about it. And we were aware that there were kinds of people. I specifically knew through the television medium that there were people who had ideas about conducting propaganda and such-like on the ground. There was very little that you ever saw that could in any way relate to this, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to offer that for tender now. It will -- it can't be tendered through this witness, but I just want to offer it for tender to give it a MFI number at this stage and see whether I can tender a basis for it at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Not if it's just for identification at this time. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's all we ask at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's have a MFI number of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI 375.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm grateful for that. Now could we please go back to the video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly there's another -- I'm sorry. Just a moment. We can't see it.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I don't know which one to press.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will be assisted there.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: That one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could we just move on from this. We're now going to come to another individual person at whom I want to stop. Yes. Play it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That person depicted there, is that the same person that we saw lying in the open just a frame or so before?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And with that picture there you can see at least one significant wound?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the wound that you recall seeing?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Could we keep playing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. That can be stopped now, thanks. And, yes, those are the -- those are the parts of the video that I wish to play to this witness. So I'm grateful to the Prosecution for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I -- you asked me if there was any blood under the woman on the carpet. You can see it in that shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I certainly will go back, then, please.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes, that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, so, if you notice something you can see --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes, you asked me if I could see any blood. In fact, there is the blood to the left of the head, very definitely, and possibly to the right, and that is congealed blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's your evidence. Do you recall that or are you basing it on what you can see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I'm basing it on what I can see, and that is a shot taken by my cameraman. Which we would not show because of its close-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I understand that, but what I'm asking you is: Do you have a specific memory of that being blood, or are you just going on what you can see in the picture?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I don't quite get that because I'm saying that I was standing next to my cameraman most of the time, and that is blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: What else would it be?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm asking -- well, I don't know what else it would be, but I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I suggest it is blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay, because -- just attend to the question for a second. At the time did you know it was blood or is it something that you're now saying you noticed --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I would know at the time it was blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, just to make sure of that we'd better play on with that scene because there may be something that confirms what you say or not.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There does not appear to be blood elsewhere that we can see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. That can be stopped now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, after you had visited those houses -- let me just ask you a question about this. Did you -- do you recall one hamlet that was -- we know -- we know the name of it is Kriz, but do you recall there being a hamlet on the side of a hill detached from the others by perhaps 500 metres or so?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No, not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any village point -- any neighbouring village high up on a ridge pointed out to you as being a Muslim-inhabited village called Here?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No, but it was a mixed area. I was aware of the composition around Prozor, where you had a scattering of both Muslim and Croat villages in that area, and they would be within sight of each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, after you had finished at -- in the -- the hamlets, did you go back to the school?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We went first to the hamlets, then we ended up at the school. That is where we finally were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were at the school, you noticed a particular wall which had some blood on it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was obvious to you that that wall had been wiped in some form or cleaned in some form; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: It appeared to be. That's -- it wasn't running blood, but it was smeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yet the -- but that blood that was on the wall wasn't limited to one small part but seemed to be covering quite a significant area of the wall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: It was and the floor had, we think, been clear -- cleaned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because the floor was spotless?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that, but it appeared not to have any traces of any large amounts of blood on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did any of the Croatian militiamen who were present give you any account of how that all came about?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We had no good evidence. There was by that time through the various remarks made in Prozor and by bits and pieces suggested by the British soldiers who had an interpreter and the two monitors, that clearly something had taken place, we think prior to the killings of the elderly people, and that the school which was said to be a Croat HQ had been involved. I can't be more specific than that. I felt at the time very worried that I could not get more information. It's a very uncomfortable position to be in, and there was no hard evidence of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- were you able to speak to local journalists and local media people and --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: There weren't any. What local journalists? There were no newspapers. There's no radio, no television. There were no local journalists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: What a fantasy. This is -- this is a chaotic country. These institutions and sources of information do not exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't tune your radio into an institution called Radio Rama at any stage?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Not journalism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm just talking about the existence of the --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: All three sides had propaganda outfits which peddled rubbish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- I understand you're not preferring one side to the other here. I'm not asking you to do so. But I -- my questions relate to the Croat -- Croatian or HVO media outlets because that's what is relevant to this case. Did you have the experience that those media outlets would simply put out whatever information they thought assisted their cause?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Including putting out what they had made up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that false or exaggerated claims about atrocities were put out over those media outlets?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: With so much frequency we never listened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your professional position was that it just wasn't really worth paying any attention to those outlets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: You could, but you would need to monitor it 24 hours a day and have good local information to verify specific claims made because of the very nature of the way the information was delivered, which was frequently hysterical and aggressive and totally without reason, it was -- it would have been a full-time monitoring job for a team of professionals to sift relevant and good information from any of those outlets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- very well. If you were to perform that sort of sifting exercise, intelligence gathering on --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: That's not intelligence gathering. Monitoring on that scale, and I speak from the biggest monitoring organisation in the world, the BBC, is -- would have been near impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, I think you've really answered the question there. And to put it in a colloquial term, what you heard on the Croatian radio, that just wasn't really news, was it, as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We would not see it as a news source, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you for that. Now, I think I'm going to have to go into the closed session for this -- for this document, Your Honour. Would -- might I just ask that we go into the closed session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, this is what you said in the statement concerning some conclusions that you drew from at -- at Prozor. You said that you -- I think you've answered that. I'm sorry, I won't trouble you with that, actually. You've answered that question. You indicated as to the conclusions that you drew in your article some of the -- or the bases upon which you based those comments. Now, I just want to put those to you and ask you some questions about them. You said this in your statement, "I did not see any mutilated, tortured, beaten, or burnt bodies," and that is the fact isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. None of the bodies had any restraints on them? That's the fact too?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The houses had not been looted, that's the fact?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Can I also put another word in? They had not been -- looted is not the correct word in one sense. In that area, it was our experience that when houses were in any way attacked, they would have the contents broken and thrown out the windows, piled in heaps on the lawn, smashed, and in every way damaged and ruined. It was rare to see looting going on, but there was no evidence of what I suppose we call trashing a house. That is the more-specific term I should have used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By trashing, do you mean that sort of contemptuous --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Effectively degrading the enemy's will --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as conquering his village?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes. There may not -- the one conclusion I might have drawn from that is that there may not have been time. I got the impression that they had gone into -- that there was such a pattern of killing that it was a house-to-house system that went -- was used, and there wasn't time to hang around. Which suggests that these people did not intend to hold the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that some of the villagers had been taken by Muslim soldiers known to them, as a matter of fact, and kept in a cellar and let go later on. Did anyone bring that --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No one mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as to the people that were killed in the open, did it occur to you whether or not those people were in the company of armed HVO soldiers when they were killed?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Any soldier who ran across an open field with a bunch of fighters trying to shoot you would be stupid. Terrified elderly people might just run. A soldier would not go across an open field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By soldier do you mean a --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: A fighter. If he had any brains he would not be running across an open field, about the worst defensive tactic you could manage. I assumed those were terrified elderly people who ran for their lives. To be accompanied by military people you would have defiled by a lane into a wood, along a hedgerow or whatever. No soldier would run across an open field. No young man with any military experience would do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What if he didn't have a choice?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I can't see -- you don't choose death. You try the best option.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you be prepared to concede this, that you and I can put scenarios to each other but we're in the realm of speculation?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: We are, but not with that. You would not -- I haven't -- soldiers do not run across open fields when there are people waiting to shoot them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we agree with this: I put to you that you're a hundred per cent wrong and you say you're a hundred per cent right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: But I have one --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Can I make one point about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: All this is becoming very argumentative. There is no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, I just think -- I think the witness in fairness is giving her views of things. The Prosecution was allowed to lead that evidence by the Court and the Defence doesn't agree with it, but that's about as far as it goes. I think I'm not proposing to engage the witness in a dispute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I -- I -- and I recognise I'm speculating. All I'm trying to put over is that it was a chaotic, irregular, badly disciplined, if anything, conflict. And in these instances, you can't rely on what people would do under conventional conflict circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just excuse me for one moment, please, Ms. Adie.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those are the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time for the lunch break, so we might come back at 2.30. Is that agreeable? We only have two minutes left for the morning session. Yes. We will resume at 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just two questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Re-examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Adie.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just two questions. One is, you were questioned by Defence counsel about your hearing that Bosnian police officers were involved. However, when you gave your broadcast some hours later, you opened up by saying "the Bosnian army descended on Uzdol," and then a little later "every house and cottage had been visited by the Bosnian army soldiers." Were did you use the phrase "Bosnian army"?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Because the Bosnian army would be recognised by my audience as an overarching organisation to which any action which had any militaristic context would be ascribed. In other words, we did not, unless we had a very, very specific bit of information, give different names to different groups, even though it might seem more accurate to people locally. We would just refer to "the Bosnians" or "the Bosnian army." There were times when we made a specific difference here and there, but on the whole we would say "the Bosnians" or "the Bosnian army."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other question I had was, you were asked about some of your conclusions towards the end of the cross-examination, and it -- you answer on page 117, you have an answer, "Absolutely," as to whether or not trashing means some sort of contempt for the people. And then the question, it says, "Key grade," and it's -- the question basically is none -- is unintelligible, and your answer is "Yes, the one conclusion I might have drawn from that is there may not have been time. I get [sic] the impression that they'd gone in, that there had been a pattern of killing, that it was a house-to-house system." I don't know if you meant systematic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Systematically going from house to house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And went -- and "there wasn't time to hang around." Could you -- since it didn't come out well, could you explain, if you recall, where you were heading on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Before the witness explains that, Your Honours, I've got an objection to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I objected at the start. Your Honours indicated, if I may so, in a common-sense way that -- let's just see how the evidence goes. The witness is entitled to answer questions responsively and honestly, and no doubt has done so. But it just can't assist the Tribunal. Some of the things that have been said here are, you know, may be valid in other forums, but to engage in what the witness herself prepared to say seem to be entering into the realms of speculation now is just not going to assist the Tribunal. I'm not attacking the bona fides of it. What I'm objecting to is the question and the attempt to elicit another version of that -- that same account. This house-to-house pattern of killing and so on is just unadmissable, unhelpful in any way in court proceedings, so I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe the question put by the Prosecution is not a proper one because you asked the witness to explain where she was heading on that. But however, I believe that the question put by the Prosecution is mainly within the scope of the clarification on that issue. On this point, I will allow the witness to clarify it, what she means by "systematically."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The question was, since it's not clear from the transcript, what do you mean by systematic, the systematic house to house and not enough time? It's just not clear from this answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: What I meant was that in many villages I'd been in before where people had been killed and where houses had been damaged, there was much greater damage and a sense that people had come into the village and had taken possession of it. That used to happen with ethnic cleansing and at times when front lines, so-called, moved forward and back, that you went in and you stamped your mark on it. You burnt houses, you trashed belongings, you threw things out of the windows. You made the houses uninhabitable. It's part of territorial acquisition. In this instance, that hadn't happened, it seemed to me. Whoever had come in had not stayed to do that, had not spent time doing that, which we'd seen all over the place. They had come in, but a considerable number of people had been killed individually in situ in different houses over several -- well, over a few hundred yards and more, and also a couple in fields, and I had the sense that they had been determinedly sought out, looked for in their houses, because they were inside, upstairs, in a bed. This -- that says to me -- and systematically what I mean by that is someone must have take the decision. And I don't know if we're talking individually or an order, I have no idea, but someone must have taken a decision and a voice must have been raised saying, "Kill whoever you can find." That was what was going on. That's what it seemed to me to be, and that these people had to be found to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions from the Bench? Judge El Mahdi. Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Mrs. Adie, I would -- I understand that you understand French as well as you do English. I would just like to clarify a number of points and relating to your testimony. The first has to do with misinformation or information misconstrued. You stated that the parties to the conflict were trying, whenever possible, to provide misleading information, and you excluded the possibility of saying that what you had seen had been manipulated. No. You said that what you had seen was in fact what had happened. So whilst being aware of the fact that misleading information was provided to you by the parties to the conflict, how can you ascertain as relates to this particular incident that what you had seen was not something that had been arranged but was actually truthful?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: It's a very valid point, and I was very aware of it when I went into the village, partly because we were accompanied by some Croat men in uniform. Clearly also Croats had been into the village from outside to bring down the corpses to Prozor, and we were 24 hours after the event at least. I'm totally aware of that. And I was looking for signs of a stage-managed scene, and I have seen this before in other conflicts. From what we saw of the bodies, it seemed to me that they had been killed where they lay. Admittedly, blankets had been put round people. They would have had to move a body. But at no point did I see what I could -- and I have to say in many instances we were dealing with unsophisticated military outfits. At no point did I see any, what I might say, dramatic, overexaggerated poses and positions, any what I would call in television terms a display of the bodies. You would look for that. You would look for someone making a dramatic gesture. And they seemed to me, and we had to look for the bodies, to be lying pretty well where they were killed. So I wasn't conscious of any major manipulation. It is possible to say that by putting blankets round, maybe something was being concealed, but I couldn't see what. We could see the injuries. We saw people's physical position as they had been killed. There was no, as I call it, sometimes sentimental rearrangement of the body. I have seen this before. It seemed to me pretty realistic. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. My second question runs as follows: Some bodies were taken to Prozor, others remained in the spot where they allegedly had been killed. Did anybody tell you how these bodies were sorted, which ones were taken away? Where were these bodies that had been taken away, and why did some remain, and why did others get taken away? Did anybody provide any explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever. It was puzzling to us as to why you would bring some bodies out and why you would leave others there. I have no idea. I -- no one told us, and no one gave any explanation. And it's -- I could speculate, but I don't think it would be constructive. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Fine. My last question has to do with what you mentioned. You mentioned the school. You said that at the school you noticed some signs of fighting, of an exchange of fire, and this had been cleaned up, that there were traces of blood on the walls, but that the floor was clean, which means, in other words, and this is -- was what I would like you to confirm, that someone had cleaned the place up. Someone had cleaned the place up, had cleaned the school, but had not cleaned other places up. You were accompanied by Croat members of the army. Did they tell you why some places -- one place had been cleaned up and why other places had not been cleaned up? Was this to clearly demonstrate or is it that they wanted to show you something quite specific?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I -- at that point -- at that point I had deep misgivings about what had been going on. I felt adrift. I felt very, very concerned, because I wondered myself what had happened in the school. I wondered if people had been executed there. That was my first thought, the number of bodies I'd seen in Prozor. But on the other hand, there was no example of using automatic fire and a lot of bullets and torn clothing and -- which you probably would have seen in an execution. I had no idea. I'd found the whole atmosphere, I will be candid, hugely disturbing. That someone had cleaned a place seemed to be unnatural and suspect -- one suspects, a cover-up. What is someone trying to hide? I could get no answer for this. I didn't know. I had a very uneasy feeling that I would never know what went in, in time for broadcast, and my responsibility as a journalist is to get that news out that night as accurately as possible with as many facts, and I knew I was not going to get that information. When someone has cleaned up a room and there are other people lying unburied in the village, what is going on? And I have no answer to that. It makes me feel extremely diffident, but it didn't alter my view of those people in the houses. I sense that that was quite clear to me, what might have happened. What happened in the school I have -- I do not know. And the fighting was alluded to by the British army soldiers, and they gave me the phrase, when I said, "Can you tell from the gunfire -- gunfire damage what happened," they said it looks like a rear guard action, and I took their testimony there. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] My last question has to do with the state of these bodies. I know this is rather unpleasant, but in what condition were these bodies? The bodies in Prozor, were they in the same condition as others? Can you confirm that these bodies or that these people had been killed at the same time, in other words, on the 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN ADIE
utterances.text: I do not have the professional expertise to give a time of death. There seemed to be no substantial difference in the state of the bodies that I saw in Prozor and in Uzdol to my amateur eye, no major difference. They were all wrapped in the same kind of clean blankets, and I rather suspected that those blankets had come from one source. We're talking a couple of dozen very clean blankets, and all the bodies had been wrapped in these similar blankets. The gunshot wounds seemed to be of the -- what had happened to the bodies appeared to be the same. I had no reason, but I have no proof that they all died in roughly the same time. I don't have the proof. I can't prove it. But I saw no difference between the groups. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge El Mahdi. Any questions out of Judge El Mahdi's questions? It seems to me there are none. At this stage, are there any documents to tender on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Ours are all tendered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There's one that we offered for tender, Your Honour, which is not in a state to be tendered yet. I don't seek to tend it now through this witness, as I indicated, so that could just be in abeyance until we make our case about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. But anyway, it has a number on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So that we won't miss it. There will be an announcement about the correction of the numbers of the documents by the court deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There's one document that was tendered under seal, and it was wrongly described as Prosecution Exhibit. In fact, it's a Defence Exhibit and it will have the number D376, which will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. We wish you a very pleasant journey, and Madam Usher will show you out of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may go now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to say. We've got a bit of a problem, I think, with the LiveNote. On my computer here, it's -- we've got the old version that's working right now but we just -- the Ringtail version of the transcript is not working on my computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. But mine's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I can see actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe we could ask a technician to have it fixed. So are we ready to hear the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I think so, Your Honour. If it starts to cause trouble, I'll say, and meanwhile we should press on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karavelic. Some formal questions. Your name is Vahid Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born on the 7th of April, 1956?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You describe yourself as a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: I had different nicknames in my life, but of late they've been calling me Vaha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they call you Vaha in the war?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes, very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your occupation, you're a retired major general.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you retire on the 31st of August last year from a very senior position, which was about number three in the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the formal title of your position at the time of your retirement?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Chief of the administration for policy, plans, and operations attached to the staff of the joint command of the Federation army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this the third time that you have testified in proceedings before the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you testify for the Prosecution in the case of Prosecutor against Galic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recently, that is last month, testify for the Defence as an expert witness, a military expert witness, in the case of Prosecutor versus Hadzihasanovic and Kubura?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the relevant time during the war with which -- which concerns this indictment, were you the commander of the 1st Corps in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: I was the assistant commander of the 1st Corps until mid 1993, and as of August 1993, I was the commander of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly to take you back to the point where you got to there to enable the Trial Chamber to understand your military background and expertise. Did you join the JNA in 1975 and graduate from the military academy in Belgrade in 1979?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a platoon commander from 1979 to 1982, rising to the rank of second lieutenant and then lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you then based in Ljubljana as the deputy commander of an elite motorised battalion in the 1980s?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes. Deputy commander of the militarised battalion. That's right. I think there was a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And from 1988 to 1991, were you the commander of that same battalion?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Until 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you move to then?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: After the armed conflicts, namely the aggression against the Republic of Slovenia, Belgrade decided, the top military leadership in Belgrade, decided to relocate all the armed formations of the Yugoslav People's Army from the territory of the Republic of Slovenia to the central parts of the remainder of Yugoslavia. At that time, my brigade and I myself with my battalion were relocated from the barracks in Ljubljana to the barracks in Zenica. More precisely, this took place on the 20th of August, 1991. And then two months later, precisely on the 20th of October, 1991, I was relocated, just me with my battalion, that is, to the Tuzla barracks, from Zenica to Tuzla. The intention being of my being sent to attack the city of Vukovar in the north-eastern part of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And was it as a result of that intention that you in fact left or, in military terms, deserted the JNA in 1991, at the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of December, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join the Patriotic League in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Not in Visoko, yes, but I did join the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Sefer Halilovic at that time its deputy leader?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes, he was, and he and the late General Karesik, they actually admitted me to the league.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Sefer Halilovic then?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Not until that time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April 1992, were you appointed to the command of the Territorial Defence in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: In April 1992, on the 12th and 13th of April, 1992, after the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an internationally recognised state, and after the establishment of the new army in Bosnia and Herzegovina called the Territorial Defence, which was on the 8th of April, 1992, after several days I was appointed the commander of the District Territorial Defence of the Municipality of Tuzla, and I was also a member of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm trying to get through this reasonably briefly. If you could possibly help me with this, because I think I can lead on this: Were you captured by Serb forces on the 27th of April, 1992, and taken to Sremska Mitrovica military prison near Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated, court-martialed by the Serb -- or the JNA, sentenced to death?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, 1992, were you transferred to -- by helicopter to Pale near Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Four days later were you exchanged for some high-ranking Serb or JNA military officials?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes. They were from the security service. They were the assistants to the first man, the leading man of that particular service in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following your exchanges were you placed on the Main Staff of the fledgling Bosnian army from May 1992 until August 1992?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: After a short time of recovery, I was attached to the republican Territorial Defence -- Defence Staff commanded by Hasan Efendic. And then towards the end of May that same year, after this duty was assumed by General Sefer Halilovic, I also continued doing the same work in the command with Sefer Halilovic at the helm until I was appointed the deputy commander of the 1st Corps, which was on the 1st of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it Sefer Halilovic who recommended or arranged your appointment to the Main Staff? I'm sorry, the Territorial Republican Defence.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I do think that he did, that it was him. In fact, prior to the appointment of General Sefer Halilovic, I was already a member of the Republican TO Staff while Efendic was the commander. And after Mr. -- General Halilovic assumed the post of commander of TO, I continued doing the same -- performing the same duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 1st Corps in Sarajevo when you were appointed as deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Until that time, there had existed a District or Regional, and both are quite correct, Staff in Sarajevo, just like there had existed a District and Regional Staff in Tuzla where I was until I was arrested and captured. At the helm of this was Hajrulahovic Mustafa, nicknamed Talijan, the Italian. After the creation of the 1st Corps of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or rather the 1st Corps in Sarajevo he was appointed commander and I was appointed his deputy. That was on the 1st of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're on this, are you a cousin of a person called Hasan Cengic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: No. No, no. No relation whatsoever. No kinship whatsoever with this person. Nor did I know him at all until the Patriotic League time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was -- from your last -- the answer before the last one, were you saying that the 1st Corps was created on about the 1st of September, 1992, that is it didn't exist before then?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: That is exactly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Well, it changed from time to time. Initially this zone of responsibility, according to the first variant when the corps were constituted and established within the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the -- that zone encompassed the city of Sarajevo proper, its immediately surroundings, and the entire territory to the east up to the state border on the Drina River, meaning including Gorazde, Rudo, Visegrad, and even Zepa and Sokolac, and so on and so forth, and Pale as well. Later this changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of spring/summer 1993, had its area of responsibility contracted?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: There is a part of the territory in the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina that did contract, but there was another part that was added to it containing an operations group at Visoko which had been part of the 3rd Corps up to that point. It was several times detached from the 1st Corps and then brought back to the organic composition of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Trial Chamber about the composition of the 1st Corps or the structure of the 1st corps as of spring/summer 1993, from the corps command with you and Talijan as the commander and deputy commander, the corps structure, the chief of staff, the brigades, the subordination, the departments within it. First of all, was the corps structure of the 1st Corps the same as the corps structure of all the other corps in the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Most frequently and for the most part the organisation and structure of all corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and especially as concerns the corps commands, were the same, which means nearly identical. Depending on the manpower of a certain corps, the command, too, would be established. It depends on the extent to which the different bodies within a corps were manned or short staffed. For example, the 1st Corps of the BH army in Sarajevo, of which I was commander, throughout 1993, for example, the manpower levels changed. There used to be about 75.000 soldiers. That's what the corps numbered. It was only natural that the corps command should include more members than, for example, the corps command of the 4th or 5th Corps, which had a maximum of perhaps 15.000 soldiers each within their composition. Generally speaking, however, the structure of corps commands was -- specifically the structure of the 1st Corps command was always follows: The corps commander heading the command, his deputy, the secretary, the cabinet, whatever you choose to call it, and there are several departments that are permanently in touch with the commander. First of all, the staff. The most numerous body and the most important subject of the corps in a manner of speaking, the chief would be led by the chief of staff and this applies to all units from brigade level upwards. This staff would have within its composition a variety of bodies in charge of planning, monitoring and control of combat activity. The different branches were also represented in the staff. People, more specifically officers that were at the head of each of these branches. Our army, for example, had seven different branches in arms and services. You had the chief of the artillery, the chief of the armoured and mechanised units, the chief in infantry, the chief of atomic and biochemical warfare defence, the chief of communications, and so on and so forth. In addition to the chief of staff and the staff itself, and these were permanently in touch with the corps command, also in touch with the corps commander were the following bodies: Assistant commander for morale, information and propaganda, religion-related issues, all these would be discharged by a single person. The next one was assistant for security. You also had an assistant for legal matters, an assistant for logistics and an assistant for finance. Roughly speaking, this is what the corps command structure was. The corps command would sometimes comprise as few as 50 or 60 people, or this figure could go up to 150 people depending on the size of each corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were each of these assistant commanders directly subordinated to you as the corps commander or whoever the corps commander was?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: The ones that I've mentioned would have been directly in touch with the corps commander or, rather, subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the assistant for security? Was he subordinated both to you and to the military security service?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Unlike all these assistants, the assistant for security --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have had some evidence on this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Don't interrupt the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I object to my friend's -- the witness is going to give us an explanation of something we already have had a significant amount evidence on. I just want a very, very short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I submit that the witness be giving a chance to give a responsive answer to the question that he's asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It depends on whether the witness has finished his answer or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I agree Your Honour, we should ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We may ask the witness whether he has finished his answer or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would appear that you haven't actually finished your answer, but I would very much appreciate a very brief answer to the -- to the proposition I put to you.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: If you look at all the assistants that report to the corps commander, the assistant commander for security was the most peculiar position on account of the nature of this person's work, of the incumbent's work. When I say peculiar, what I have in mind is one very important matter. All the assistants, for example, within a corps command in one way or another reported to their superiors, to their relevant -- respective superiors at a higher command level, but only as far as professional matters go. However, the assistant for security, and I'm talking about an institution that on a personal level, as a military professional, I never approved of. But this is how it worked, the security service. The assistant for security would only inform the corps commander about whatever he -- he saw fit and whatever he believed was relevant. He had no duty or explicit obligation to inform about everything. However, he would send all of the information to his own superior within the security service to a higher level position and in turn he would receive instructions from his own superior. Bottom line, in addition to the official chain of command within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, the situation must be similar in a lot of other armies throughout the world, a lot of other military forces, there was another chain of command that was peculiar to the security service and practically ran parallel to the official or main chain of command, if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to give directions or orders to your assistant for security?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have to obey them?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: He did, yes, and this was most often the case but by no means always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What circumstances did he not obey your orders?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say. Specifically, I as commander of the 1st Corps in a great number of situations was in no position to know what my assistant for security was doing specifically, what sort of task he was performing at a given time. It was only much later once everything was over and done with that I would learn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the structure, did you have a military police battalion attached to the corps command as opposed to at the brigade level?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that subordinated to and what was its strength?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Military Police Battalion was in the same category as any other unit that was attached to the staff. Every corps had several units attached to the staff, units of four or five different types. The Military Police Battalion was only one of those units that were attached to the staff. As a norm, a Military Police Battalion would number, although you have to take into account the fact that manpower levels were never quite identical, but usually it was between 300 and 400 men, sometimes more, sometimes less. This changed over time. When I say units attached to the staff, I mean that in a formal sense. Those units were under the command of the corps, but they also reported to the chief of staff, to his chiefs for the different branches and arms and services. Specifically talking about the Military Police Battalion, the Military Police Battalion was a unit meant to carry out tasks, to carry out instructions given by the assistant chief for security. They are the ones who know the situation, who are in a position to give good, well-founded instructions on what the Military Police Battalion should be doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they reported to the chief of staff. Do you mean the chief of staff of the corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: In the case of many other units attached to the staff, yes, to the chief of the staff of the corps, but the military police battalion commander answered or reported to the chief of security and to the corps commander too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you issue orders or directions to the military police directly or did that have to go through your assistant -- sorry, your chief of security?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Yes, but this was not done in practice. The reason was that it was highly unclear what the competence was of a chief of corps to impart good and clear orders to the military police battalion to carry out such-and-such investigation or perhaps an on-site investigation or other such tasks. So the corps commander would do it through his own chief of security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your chief of security Mr. Sacir Arnautovic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: For a while, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say when the corps commander would do it through his own chief of security, can you please explain? Do you mean that you would direct or ask or task or order the chief of security to do it or would something else happen?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: Precisely. I would order my chief of security to do this or that, and then he would use his own officers from his own department and carry out the tasks. And in order to execute any other tasks he would always have the military police battalion at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the chief of staff of the 1st Corps in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: At the beginning, I think, but I'm not sure for how long, it was Asim Dzambasovic, followed Alija Ismet, who in turn was followed by Nedzad Ajnadzic, and I'm talking about 1993. So three different chiefs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to the brigades. How many brigades were subordinated to the 1st Corps command in 1993? First I just want the number, and then I want you to name them. That's all I want you to tell us.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC:
utterances.text: We talk about units, the level doesn't matter whether we're talking about a brigade or a battalion. Throughout 1993, the 1st Corps of the BH army, although this changed over time, had nearly 30 units reporting to it, including those in Sarajevo as well as those outside Sarajevo. If I take into account -- well, and depending on when exactly, because I think it was in the spring that the East Bosnian Operations Group Gorazde was detached from the organic composition of the 1st Corps, then obviously the number shrank. Up to that point, there had been about 30 brigades alone that reported to the corps.
